author: Brett
description: Brett's Box is a maker's lab notebook: an old Roomba turned into a mapping robot, a self-hosted homelab, and a 3D printer that keeps all of it held together.
blog_description: Build notes from the bench: what I tried, what broke, what I measured and what finally worked.

vslam.alt: Screen recording of the Roomba's web dashboard while it explores on its own: a grey-scale camera view on the left, and on the right a top-down map that grows as the robot drives, with its planned path drawn in purple and obstacles in red.
vslam.caption: The robot exploring on its own. Left: what the camera sees. Right: the map it builds as it goes, with the planned path in purple and obstacles in red.

twin.alt: Isaac Sim recording of the simulated Roomba driving through the simulated house on its own. A follow camera shows the robot on the carpet; panels on the right show the robot's camera view and a depth heat map, red for near and blue for far, with a legend from 0.3 to 7 metres.
twin.caption: The robot's real software exploring the simulated house on its own. Right: what its camera sees, and the depth it gets, red near to blue far. Black is outside the camera's 0.3–7 m range.

home.tagline: Robots, homelab and 3D printing, built at the bench and written down as I go.
home.intro: I like taking old hardware that most people would throw out and teaching it new tricks. This is my lab notebook: the wiring diagrams, the dead ends, the measurements and the small wins.
home.featured_summary: A 2007-era Roomba 550 with a Jetson Orin Nano and a stereo depth camera on its back. It builds a map of the house with visual SLAM, plans its own routes with Nav2 and explores rooms it has never seen.
home.video_caption: Live from the robot's dashboard: exploring and mapping on its own, no remote control.
now: Developing navigation algorithms in Isaac Lab, starting with teaching the robot to get itself unstuck in a simulated copy of the house.
Taking the robot's new Rust nodes on their first real drive: ten of them, a fraction of the CPU of the Python originals.
Recording test drives to compare the CPU (Basalt) and GPU (cuVSLAM) pipelines' maps side by side.
Wiring an ADS1115 pack-voltage monitor so the robot parks itself before the Ridgid pack runs flat.
Still hunting the cause of Charging Error 3 (next step: borrow an oscilloscope).
